strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper convincingly identifies two concrete limitations of 3DGS-based language fields (spatial ambiguity from overlapping Gaussians, multi-level semantic ambiguity from mask pooling) and designs its method around them.

The switch to SVRaster as a structured, disjoint geometric backbone is a sensible and well-argued design choice that enables deterministic, batch-parallel feature fusion and avoids the memory bottlenecks of 3DGS registration (claimed O(1) memory and ~3 min feature lifting).

Strong empirical results: new state-of-the-art on LERF 3D object retrieval (56.11 mIoU / 85.21 Acc@25) and large gains on ScanNet open-vocabulary point cloud segmentation (+21.56 mIoU over Dr. Splat), with consistent improvements across class granularities.

Comprehensive ablation study (Table 4) that traces each component's contribution, plus a supplementary analysis (Table 6, App. A) that explains *why* learned upsamplers degrade zero-shot retrieval — a useful insight beyond the main result.

Significant practical efficiency gains: ~8x faster preprocessing and much faster feature lifting than distillation baselines, with efficiency measured on comparable hardware and honest reporting of the effort needed to reproduce the Dr. Splat baseline.
Broad evaluation coverage (3D retrieval, 2D localization, point cloud understanding) and extra application demonstrations (KITTI-360 segmentation, 3D scene editing) in the supplementary.
Appropriate attribution: the paper is explicit about which components are adopted from prior work (SVRaster, AM-RADIO, SCRA/SCGA from RADSeg, losses from DNGaussian/MonoSDF).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the contribution is primarily a well-engineered integration of existing components (SVRaster, AM-RADIO dense tokens, RADSeg's SCRA/SCGA, existing depth/normal losses). Notably, the largest single ablation gain comes from the borrowed SCRA/SCGA modules (+6.32 mIoU), raising questions about which parts are genuinely novel versus transplanted. As an Applied/Systems contribution this is acceptable, but the framing as a 'paradigm shift' overstates it.

Ablation results contain a concerning anomaly: adding sliding window + Gaussian weighting *decreases* mIoU below raw RADIO features (49.79 vs 51.19), and the final performance is recovered by borrowed attention modules. The narrative that the proposed upsampling module is validated 'empirically' is thus partially contradicted by the paper's own numbers.

Claims of state-of-the-art 'across diverse 2D and 3D benchmarks' are overstated for 2D: Table 2 shows LESV below LangSplatV2 and GAGS on most scenes, with the average retrieval mIoU (56.84) below LangSplatV2 (59.88) and localization essentially tied. The 2D result should be framed as competitive, not superior.

The evaluation protocol is modified in ways that could affect fairness: a 'normalized cosine similarity metric for all methods' is introduced for 3D thresholding, and the ScanNet protocol is adapted from ProFuse with custom candidate weighting (including removal of Mahalanobis gating based on the authors' own observation). These deviations, while motivated, weaken strict comparability with previously published numbers and are not validated by showing that original protocols yield similar rankings.

Missing baselines in the point cloud comparison: no comparison against established open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods outside the 3DGS family (e.g., OpenScene, PLA, ConceptFusion, or scene-level VLM approaches like SceneSplat, which is cited but not compared), making the ScanNet SOTA claim narrower than presented.

Presentation sloppiness undermines confidence: a broken cross-reference ('Figure ??' in Sec. 4.3), inconsistent citation numbering (LangSplat as [19]/[12], Dr. Splat as [7]/[13] in Fig. 9), duplicate CLIP references [20]/[21], and typos ('Sliglip2'). For a camera-ready-quality venue these should not persist.

Reproducibility details are thin: key hyperparameters (kernel bandwidth β, confidence decay σ, sliding window size/stride, thresholds) are not specified, and no code release is mentioned despite the efficiency claims being a central selling point.

Robustness of the method is only demonstrated on relatively small, reconstructed indoor scenes plus one qualitative KITTI-360 demo; quantitative evaluation on large-scale or unbounded outdoor scenes is absent, leaving the scalability claims (e.g., O(1) memory) empirically under-supported.

strengths: The paper identifies two concrete limitations of 3DGS-based language field registration (spatial ambiguity of overlapping Gaussians and multi-level semantic ambiguity of mask-pooled features) and motivates them clearly.

The combination of a structured SVRaster backbone with a deterministic, confidence-gated multi-view fusion rule (Eq. 2, 5, 6) is technically sensible, and the claim of O(1)-memory batched fusion is a practically useful property if verified.

Comprehensive experiments: 3D object retrieval and point cloud segmentation (Tables 1, 3) show large gains over Dr. Splat, with a reasonable ablation (Table 4) that isolates the contribution of geometric regularization, depth confidence, sliding-window upsampling, and the SCRA/SCGA modules; efficiency numbers (Table 5) are compelling.

Useful supplementary material: the multi-level TSDF fusion algorithm is specified precisely, the analysis of deep upsampler degradation is a genuinely interesting empirical finding, and real-world KITTI-360 demos suggest practical applicability.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the work is primarily an assembly of existing components — SVRaster [25] for geometry, AM-RADIO [22] dense patch tokens, RADSeg's SCRA/SCGA modules, DN-Gaussian-style depth/normal losses, and Dr.Splat-style registration. The individual design decisions (depth-weighted averaging, sliding-window inference, patch-level depth normalization) are all standard. The main novelty reduces to applying a known backbone to a known task with known fusion heuristics, which is more of an engineering contribution than an algorithmic or conceptual advance.

Overclaiming relative to the evidence. The abstract claims 'new state-of-the-art across diverse 2D and 3D benchmarks', yet Table 2 shows LangSplatV2 clearly beats the method on average 2D retrieval mIoU (59.88 vs 56.84) and on 2 of 4 scenes, and Table 1 shows the method loses decisively to Dr. Splat on the figurines scene (mIoU 55.87 vs 61.73) and to Dr.Splat/OpenGaussian on waldo_kitchen mIoU. The claims should be scoped precisely; several statements in Secs. 4.2/4.5 read as promotional rather than scientific.

Evaluation protocol modifications are introduced favoring the method without sufficient justification. The authors change thresholding to a 'normalized cosine similarity metric for all method evaluated' and admit baseline thresholds are 'sub-optimal' for their features; the effect of this protocol change on baseline numbers is not analyzed. Similarly, the ScanNet protocol removes Mahalanobis gating from the baseline 'as we empirically observed' with no supporting numbers, and point-cloud transfer uses different candidate counts for the baseline (K=64) vs. their method (K=8) — asymmetric treatment that undermines the claimed +21 mIoU gap.

A broken cross-reference ('Figure ??' in Sec. 4.3) indicates an unfinished manuscript; there are additional copy-editing issues ('groud truth', 'Sliglip2', inconsistent Fig. 1 legend 'Ours' vs 'LESV', Eq. 6 notation inconsistency between w_{conf,k} and w_{conf,i,k}). These suggest the paper was not carefully proofread.

The core contribution statement 'enabling highly scalable, O(1) memory processing' is asserted but never measured: no peak-memory comparison with Dr. Splat is reported, only wall-clock times (Table 5). The claim that Dr. Splat needs >256GB RAM is not substantiated.

The multi-level semantic ambiguity 'solution' (Eq. 8) is essentially an observation that AM-RADIO patch tokens happen to be language-aligned, inherited from [1]/[2]; the paper's own ablation shows raw RADIO tokens hurt mIoU and the gains actually come from the sliding-window plus SCRA/SCGA machinery, i.e., a fix for a problem the chosen backbone itself introduces.

Generalization evidence is thin: only LERF (4 scenes) and a small ScanNet subset are evaluated; the ablation is on a single benchmark; no variance/std over runs is reported; and the qualitative claims about 'refrigerator' behavior penalized by GT are anecdotal and could equally indicate a segmentation error.

No code or supplementary implementation details sufficient for reproduction (e.g., octree level, β, σ, crop size, threshold values are absent), despite reproducibility-critical protocol deviations described above.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies two real limitations of current 3DGS-based language field registration (spatial ambiguity from overlapping Gaussians and multi-level semantic ambiguity from mask pooling), and the proposed remedy—structured SVRaster geometry plus dense AM-RADIO patch-token features—is a coherent and sensible design.

Strong empirical results: new state-of-the-art on LERF 3D object retrieval (56.11 mIoU vs. 52.67 for Dr. Splat) and a very large margin on ScanNet point cloud understanding (+21.56 mIoU over the strongest baseline), supported by qualitative evidence on multiple datasets.

Compelling efficiency story: feature lifting in ~3 minutes and preprocessing cut by over 8x, with a clear technical justification (deterministic, voxel-disjoint fusion that avoids global depth sorting), and the O(1)-memory batch fusion claim is well motivated.

Thorough and unusually honest ablation study (Table 4) that traces each component's contribution, including the interesting negative intermediate results (sliding-window upsampling degrading mIoU before SCRA/SCGA fix it), plus a supplementary analysis of why learned upsamplers (AnyUp) fail.

Good breadth of evaluation: 2D retrieval/localization, 3D retrieval, point cloud segmentation, plus qualitative extensions to KITTI-360 driving scenes and 3D scene editing, and a multi-level TSDF mesh extraction algorithm with details provided.
Per-scene results are reported transparently (Tables 1, 2), allowing readers to see weaknesses such as waldo_kitchen 2D results rather than only averages.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily an integration of existing components (SVRaster, AM-RADIO dense patch-token alignment, RADSeg's SCRA/SCGA modules, patch-wise depth/normal losses from DN-Gaussian/MonoSDF, TSDF confidence ideas from prior work). The individual technical novelty is modest; the paper's case rests mainly on system-level combination and empirical validation, which should be stated more explicitly.

Evaluation protocol fairness concerns: the authors change the similarity metric to a 'normalized cosine similarity... for all method evaluated' because of feature-distribution differences, and they modify the baseline pipelines (e.g., Dr. Splat memory management, ScanNet K-nearest protocols with K=64 vs. K=8 and dropped Mahalanobis gating). These choices could favor the proposed method; the paper should justify or ablate each protocol deviation more carefully.

Overstated claims: the abstract and contributions claim SoTA on 2D object retrieval, but Table 2 shows LESV is second-best on average mIoU (56.84 vs. 59.88 for LangSplatV2) and clearly worse on waldo_kitchen (46.24 vs. 59.10). The narrative around the 'refrigerator' query being penalized by coarse GT is interesting but risks rationalizing unfavorable results.

Presentation and correctness issues that must be fixed: a broken reference (Figure ?? in Section 4.3), inconsistent citation keys (LangSplat cited as [21] in Table 7, [19] elsewhere; Dr. Splat as [13] in Figure 9), duplicated CLIP references ([20]/[21]), and vague hyperparameter descriptions (β and σ in Eqs. 2/5 are never given values or sensitivity analysis).

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is mentioned, the implementation is tied to a specific high-end GPU ('RTX 5090-equivalent'), and several details (sliding-window stride/crop size, quantile τq, SCRA/SCGA thresholds) are absent, which would hinder reproduction.

The evaluation is limited to relatively small-scale, indoor-centric datasets for quantitative claims; the autonomous-driving experiments (Fig. 7) are purely qualitative, so the scalability claims for large unbounded scenes remain unverified quantitatively.

Novel theoretical or analytical insight is limited; the argument for why voxel-disjoint geometry removes semantic bleeding is intuitive but not analyzed (e.g., no quantitative spillover metric), and some design choices (2σ vs. 2β² normalization inconsistency between Eqs. 2/5 and 5) suggest insufficient rigor.

strengths: Well-motivated framing: the paper clearly articulates two concrete limitations of 3DGS-based feature registration (spatial ambiguity of overlapping Gaussians and multi-level semantic ambiguity from mask pooling) and designs the method around them.

Strong empirical results on open-vocabulary point cloud understanding: +21.56% mIoU on ScanNet-19 over the strongest baseline, with consistent gains on 15/10-class splits and ScanNet200; this is a substantial and convincing margin.

Compelling efficiency profile: ~22GB bounded peak memory via spatial batching (vs. 256GB for Dr. Splat), ~8× preprocessing speedup, and ~3 min feature lifting — the memory analysis (Table 6) is a genuinely useful systems contribution.

Careful ablations that disentangle representation from backbone (Table 5), validate the geometric components (Table 4), and justify the sliding-window upsampling choice over learned upsamplers (Table 8, supplementary A). This goes beyond typical 'ours beats baseline' evidence.

Extensive supplementary evaluation (ScanNet200, KITTI-360 autonomous driving, 3D scene editing, extended qualitative results), and an honest limitations section acknowledging resolution bottlenecks and lack of real-time rendering.

Appropriate attribution: the paper is transparent that SVRaster, AM-RADIO, RADSeg modules, and monocular losses are adopted from prior work and positions its contribution as the fusion/registration framework.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core ingredients (SVRaster backbone, AM-RADIO dense features, RADSeg's SCRA/SCGA, MonoSDF-style depth/normal losses) are all existing, and the paper's contribution is largely an integration pipeline. The multi-level TSDF fusion and confidence gating are the most original pieces, but their measured impact is modest (+1.44 mIoU on ScanNet, +2.57 mIoU on LERF in Table 4).

Results on 2D retrieval/localization (Table 2) and 3D object retrieval (Table 1) are mixed rather than state-of-the-art: LESV trails Occam's LGS/LangSplat-v2 on 2D retrieval mIoU and LaGa on 3D mIoU, weakening the 'new SoTA across diverse benchmarks' claim in Fig. 1; the honest but softer framing ('competitive') contrasts with the title/teaser claims.

Several protocol modifications complicate comparability: baselines were re-implemented (LangSplat, LaGa under Dr. Splat's protocol), normalized cosine similarity was introduced to align feature spaces, and Mahalanobis gating was removed from baselines based on the authors' own empirical judgment; these choices are described but not independently validated, and no code release is mentioned, which affects reproducibility.

The multi-level ambiguity resolution rests on an 'emergent' property of AM-RADIO patch tokens cited from [1] rather than a contribution of the paper; if this property is brittle across RADIO versions or heads, the approach's robustness is unclear (only 'Radio-v3' is mentioned in passing in Table 2's caption).

Minor inconsistencies and polish issues: text cites 63.84%/51.87% for ramen 2D mIoU while Table 2 reports 63.40%/51.80%; Dr. Splat is cited with conflicting reference numbers ([11] vs. [17]); the claim that geometric supervision makes voxels 'outperform' Dr. Splat is only true against the CLIP-feature variant (32.06 vs. 31.66, a 0.40 margin), which is within noise.

No evaluation of how performance scales with feature dimensionality/memory footprint for the 3D field itself (dense per-voxel embeddings presumably carry a large storage cost that is not quantified), and no discussion of societal impact beyond brief application notes.

strengths: Clear problem framing: the paper identifies two concrete failure modes of 3DGS-based language fields (spatial ambiguity from overlapping Gaussians, multi-level semantic ambiguity from mask pooling) and designs a coherent solution around them.

Strong empirical gains on open-vocabulary point cloud understanding: +21.56% mIoU over Dr. Splat on ScanNet-19, with consistent improvements across 15/10-class splits and ScanNet200 in the supplementary.

The ablations are well designed, particularly Table 5, which disentangles the representation (SVRaster vs. 3DGS) from the backbone (CLIP vs. AM-RADIO), showing the gains arise from the combination rather than the encoder alone; Table 4 isolates the geometric regularization and TSDF confidence contributions.
Notable practical efficiency: ~8x reduction in preprocessing, ~3 min feature lifting, and O(1)-memory batched fusion addressing a real 256GB RAM bottleneck of Dr. Splat.

Good coverage of tasks and benchmarks (LERF 3D/2D retrieval, ScanNet PCD, ScanNet200, KITTI-360), plus an honest limitations section discussing feature upsampling resolution and lack of real-time rendering.
The analysis of deep upsampler degradation (Appendix A) is a useful empirical finding for the community.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely integrative: SVRaster, AM-RADIO/RADSeg (SCRA/SCGA), sliding-window fusion, monocular depth/normal losses (from DNGaussian/MonoSDF), and TSDF confidence gating are existing components. The engineering is solid, but no single component is a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution; the framing as a 'paradigm shift' overstates this.

Numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: Table 2 reports ramen mIoU of 63.40, but the text cites '63.84% mIoU vs. 51.87%' and Table 1 reports ramen mIoU of 53.34; Dr. Splat is cited as [11] in most places but [17] in Fig. 9. Teatime results (69.30/84.75) are below the second-best baseline yet described as 'on par' only via averaging.

Evaluation fairness concerns: several baselines (LangSplat, LaGa, Dr. Splat) are re-implemented or modified (chunking, FP16, custom K-NN transfer protocols, normalized cosine similarity alignment), and the KNN feature-transfer protocol for ScanNet is adapted rather than standard, so cross-paper comparisons are unreliable; results rest substantially on the authors' own protocol choices.

Evidence is thin on scene diversity: the LERF benchmark contains only four scenes, and Table 6's memory analysis uses the same four scenes; the waldo_kitchen result (43.84 mIoU, below LaGa multi-level and Dr. Splat) suggests scene-dependent variance that four scenes cannot characterize.

No comparison against OpenVoxel or other SVRaster-based language methods in the main text despite being directly related (deferred to supplementary); the claim of 'state-of-the-art across diverse 2D and 3D benchmarks' in Fig. 1 is stronger than what the paper shows (only second-best average mIoU on 3D retrieval, behind LaGa multi-level in a different setting).

Reproducibility is questionable: no code release is mentioned, the multi-level SAM mask baselines and modified Dr. Splat implementation details are underspecified, and several implementation choices (beta, sigma, patch sizes, thresholds) lack sensitivity analysis.

Presentation quality is below acceptance bar in places: typos ('Sliglip2', 'segment', 'groud truth'), inconsistent reference numbering, 'Abbreviated paper title' left in the header, and some supplementary figures with vague captions.

strengths: The core idea of using Sparse Voxel Rasterization as a structured, disjoint geometry backbone for deterministic language feature registration is well-motivated and directly addresses genuine limitations (spatial ambiguity, semantic bleeding) of 3DGS-based registration methods like Dr. Splat.

The empirical evidence is strong where it matters most: a large, consistent improvement on ScanNet open-vocabulary point cloud understanding (+21.56% mIoU over Dr. Splat at 19 classes, maintained across 15/10-class splits and ScanNet200 in the supplement).

Practical efficiency claims are convincingly supported with concrete measurements (Tables 6-7): ~25GB bounded peak memory vs. 256GB+ for Dr. Splat, ~14 min preprocessing and ~3 min feature lifting, an over 8x reduction vs. LangSplat-style pipelines.

The ablation design is thoughtful, particularly Table 5, which disentangles representation (voxels vs. Gaussians) from backbone (CLIP vs. AM-RADIO), demonstrating that the gains stem from the dense registration paradigm rather than the encoder choice alone.
Multi-level TSDF fusion with confidence blending (Algorithm 1, Fig. 6) and the analysis of deep upsampler degradation (Table 8) are useful, non-obvious technical components with supporting evidence.

The limitations section is candid and substantive (feature upsampling resolution cap, no real-time novel-view feature rendering), and the supplementary covers additional benchmarks (KITTI-360, scene editing) that demonstrate generality.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely integration-level: SVRaster, AM-RADIO, patch-wise depth loss [15], normal consistency [33], and the SCRA/SCGA modules are all adopted from prior work. The genuinely new pieces (TSDF confidence gating, multi-level TSDF fusion) are incremental; the paper would benefit from more clearly delineating its own technical contribution versus assembling existing components.

Evaluation fairness is a concern: several baselines are re-implemented under modified protocols (normalized cosine similarity to 'align feature spaces', modified Dr. Splat memory management, adapted K-NN weighting for ScanNet per ProFuse). While the authors argue for fairness, these non-standard adaptations introduce reviewer-side uncertainty, and only four LERF scenes are used for retrieval, limiting statistical strength.

The headline claims slightly overreach: on LERF 3D retrieval, LESV is second-best in mIoU (56.11) and even in Table 2 it trails Occam's LGS and LangSplat-v2 in 2D retrieval mIoU; 'new state-of-the-art' properly applies to ScanNet point cloud understanding only. 'O(1) memory' is accurate only relative to scene scale, not absolutely (~25GB).

Notable unexplained anomalies: e.g., LESV's waldo_kitchen 2D mIoU (46.24) is well below baselines while ramen is well above; the refrigerator discussion admits a behavior penalized by ground truth without quantification. There are also presentation inconsistencies (Dr. Splat cited as [11] and [17] in Fig. 9, 'Sliglip2' in Fig. 2, LangSplat cited as [25] in Table 9) suggesting rushed preparation.

Key hyperparameters (Gaussian kernel bandwidth beta, confidence decay sigma, quantile/temperature for Algorithm 1, crop overlap) are not specified, and no code release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility given the heavy re-implementation of baselines.
The KITTI-360 autonomous driving experiment is purely qualitative with no quantitative benchmark, so its evidentiary value for scalability in unbounded scenes is limited.
